Urban encounters on the public realm, where individuals interact, are essential components of resilient, vibrant, and varied communities. The pandemic introduced temporary constraints on such interactions, yet it posed additional risks to urban life. This paper examines how face-to-face engagement in shared spaces evolved during the health crisis, focusing specifically on London. Drawing on data from camera traps to observe public traffic patterns, the study evaluates both the immediate and lasting impacts of pandemic restrictions. Findings indicate that while urban encounters were curtailed during lockdowns, full pre-pandemic diversity did not return; instead, social behaviors in public spaces have become more segregated, some degree of separation from pandemic effects has emerged. This research provides new insights into the consequences of the pandemic on urban life, suggesting potential threats to long-term community resilience and diversity.

This study introduces a novel, decoupled algorithm for fully coupled systems involving mass and momentum conservation within porous media applications addressing carbon capture and sequestration. Known as the Sequential coupled Mass-Separated Newton method (FSMSN), our approach decouples field equations into sequential, simplified subsets including a Sequentially coupled Fully Implicit (FSI) method for momentum and sequential fully implicit (FSLN) components for mass transfer. Unlike traditional strategy that requires solving a fully coupled system—often requiring a fully coupled solver for each subset—the FSMSN ensures the mass-balance equation remains fully coupled while solving for both mass and momentum fluxes separately using pressure as the primary coupling variable across equations. Consequently, the complex, heterogeneous nature of the CCS problem makes it ideal for this FSMSN framework that demands fewer solver resources. Numerical experiments on a 2D synthetic model demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms conventional fully coupled approaches by reducing computational time by a factor of 10 while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, results from three-dimensional (3D) simulations highlight superior performance of FSMSN in handling a realistic, 3D realistic geological formations.

Our theoretical model indicates that such a cavity amplifies interactions between chiral emitters and the field within the near-field range a vast number of times over. Furthermore, within the far-field regime, the optical power radiated by an individual emitter is amplified significantly more. In contrast to traditional metallic chiral cavities, which struggle with poor far-field radiation efficiency, this structure offers a distinct advantage by achieving strong near-field coupling without sacrificing far-field performance. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed architecture allows for highly flexible adjustments of its near-field characteristics, including coupling strength and chirality sign, simply by varying the ring coating thickness. These findings suggest that this approach offers a highly effective route for the design of future applications targeting chiral molecules and quantum technologies.

To quantify ambient heating rates for a two-dimensional Coulomb crystal within a standard single-coil Penning trap, we track shifts in the axial oscillation frequency of its isolated central ion, driven by temperature fluctuations. This study reveals a heating rate consistent with an Arrhenius model, featuring an activation energy estimated at approximately 100 meV, while maintaining a heating rate order comparable to those of nearby ions. Concurrently, we describe a novel heating rate detection system that operates without interrupting multi-ion interaction experiments. Furthermore, this methodology permits the simultaneous observation of axial frequency shifts resulting from both thermal expansion and spin interactions.

Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) is established as a established method for investigating local chemistry at a sub-molecular scale. In this study, we demonstrate that in a Cu-nanoparticle/silicon dioxide/silicon heterostructure equipped with a standard silicon TERS probe, the dominant signal originates from an electromagnetic (EM) channel rather than a chemical (CH) channel. This conclusion arises because the measured signal intensity is insensitive to changes in tip-surface gap distance and the complex optical impedance of the metal nanostructure—parameters that significantly influence the CH response—while simultaneously aligning with simulations of strongly enhanced EM scattering. Furthermore, the observed signal intensity matches predicted EM values which do not account for resonance conditions, thereby ruling out electromagnetic fluorescence as a contributing factor to our findings.

Prior research indicates that users struggle when attempting to understand a robot's intent, particularly when multiple task-input options are available and not explicitly revealed. Addressing this, our study examines user performance as well as their mental workload, stress levels, and trust across four experimental scenarios. We contrasted situations where robots communicate their objectives via display (displaying intended tasks via highlighted buttons) versus implicit communication (no display of intended tasks). Our results show that when robots make their intentions clear through a display, users complete interactions more efficiently, experience lower mental workload, and exhibit higher trust and stress levels compared to no display. Furthermore, both users and observers exhibited significantly greater efficiency, lower mental workload, and increased trust in the interaction scenario displaying the robot's intent, compared to no display.

To address the challenges associated with generating real-time global cost maps for expansive environments, this study introduces an input-output (I-O) approach to navigation. This method conveys navigation guidance through a high-level Input and a low-level Output, where inputs represent discrete discrete nodes and outputs provide continuous trajectory adjustments. An I-O controller is formulated to manage these signals, facilitating robust navigation across various scales while mitigating the heavy computational load of global navigation. Furthermore, to enhance computational efficiency, navigation nodes are adapted dynamically to nodes with higher degrees, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the input. Finally, we present HiTMap, a comprehensive representation that integrates both local and global metrics for navigation purposes. Extensive evaluations on 1,000 real-world maps obtained from the ROBO-VAL dataset confirm that a lightweight HiTMap system can effectively manage navigation on large environments.

In computed tomography (CT), image quality is often compromised by under-sampling and incomplete projections, as well as variations in detector sensitivity and scattering radiation. These issues introduce spatially dependent noise that compromises image quality. Our proposed approach employs a multi-scale image model, where image quality degradation is linked to local smoothness, combined with a state-of-the-art deep image prior network. Consequently, a single generator is used for all noise reductions across different scales. To handle the computational challenges introduced by the image prior, a fast image reconstruction is implemented using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Consequently, our method can manage scanning artifacts and noise of varying levels simultaneously. Comprehensive evaluations, supported by both synthetic data and clinical results from scans of the chest and head, demonstrate that our proposed technique outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

The light transport characteristics of a linear grating are fundamentally determined by its geometric parameters, specifically the effective gap width ($f$) and ridge width ($w$). We present analytical formulas for the effective gap width that depend on the ridge width, an inversion parameter $p$, and either the grating's depth parameter $d$ or the ridge parameter $f$. When integrated into both local and non-local predictive models, these formulations yield highly accurate results for a grating's characteristic depths and profile inversions. Testing against finite element simulations confirms that the proposed approach for estimating light effective gap widths is both precise and efficient. Compared to established local methodologies, these findings also significantly enhance the accuracy of predicting a grating's light propagation behavior.

This study introduces Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), a framework that extracts named entities from unstructured text and iteratively refines their relevance through user feedback to enhance downstream tasks. Specifically, CNER applies an exploratory search strategy to identify information about the few items selected as most promising. This feedback is leveraged to refine the retrieval approach, which is then executed to query these concepts effectively. The primary advantages of CNER are demonstrated to be superior to current state-of-the-art alternatives in exploring unknown domains within user feedback, particularly for conceptual and novel entity retrieval. The underlying framework is designed to be fully adaptable, facilitating downstream research and practical applications.

Recent advancements show that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) effectively predict patient diagnoses within task-specific silos of Electronic Health Records (EGRs). These systems model a specific EGR type as a graph to learn latent representations of its nodes and edges for a target task. However, EGRs vary widely in structure and semantics, presenting significant challenges for heterogeneous GNNs designed to process graphs of diverse types. A key difficulty lies in the lack of a unified schema, requiring models to infer node and edge meanings based on graph type, schema details, and contextual cues to achieve high performance. To address these issues, we present GraphMatch, a neural framework for multi-task learning over heterogeneous EGRs. This system jointly trains a set of graph-specific encoders—each tuned to a particular EGR type—while employing a shared decoder that aggregates encoded representations to generate predictions for associated tasks. Because these encoders are type-restricted, they need not handle all EGR types or perform every task, thereby lowering their computational demands and conceptual complexity. To facilitate communication between varying graph structures, we utilize cross-type graph matching to align nodes of different entity categories and update the shared decoder's task understanding. Our experiments across diverse clinical datasets demonstrate that GraphMatch significantly surpasses existing baselines in handling multiple heterogeneous EGR types simultaneously across multiple tasks.

This study examines numerically how the size of the counterions in the electrolyte influences the induced ordering of counterions and ions near a charged soft surface. Specifically, we identify that the density profiles of both salt and solvent exhibit oscillatory patterns whose amplitude and wavelength scale with the radius of the counterions. Based on these observations, we derive an analytical approximation for the surface concentration and surface excess within a counterion-only approximation. We clarify that this approximation remains valid under certain conditions. Additionally, we assess whether the surface excess—rather than surface charge serves as the governing factor for the electrostatic interaction energy between the surface and an approaching particle. We perform a comparison between our findings and a model originally proposed by Shenderova and Levin [J. Chem. Phys. 126, 104703 (2007)], identifying a discrepancy in their theoretical predictions regarding this interaction energy.

We assessed their performance against a baseline using an existing software dataset. Our results indicate that BERT significantly outperforms both the competition with baselines and fastText, while also revealing that training data volume is a critical factor in model efficacy.

Achieving the accurate alignment of LiWAD point clouds across multiple timestamps is crucial for constructing high-resolution environment models. Traditional methods typically rely on feature matching to establish correspondence between point clouds, but these often yield poor results when dynamic objects are present. In contrast to existing solutions tailored for static scenes, this study introduces a more effective method that reduces point-cloud density specifically in the presence of dynamics. By decreasing the amount of data processed (affecting both runtime and memory requirements), we simultaneously enhance the accuracy of feature correspondences and achieve more precise point-cloud registration compared to standard deep learning approaches to current-LIC (CC-LIC). Experimental evaluations on static and dynamic datasets confirm that our technique surpasses state-of-the-art deep learning-based registration methods in both accuracy and efficiency under all three conditions: purely static data, dynamic data tracking, and mixed environments.

Deep learning approaches are now considered highly promising for leveraging satellite imagery to derive versatile geo-information. Nevertheless, these methods face significant challenges due to varied spectral characteristics across different capture times and seasons, as well as issues with scale and resolution. This study employs a self-supervised learning framework to train representations for a multi-spectral solar wind energy prediction task using an extensive label-free multi-Gaussian dataset. By leveraging energy patterns as training objectives, the approach captures shared representations from both temporal and spectral dimensions. Evaluated against various geo-information extraction tasks, either in conjunction with inductive bias or other loss functions, it demonstrates enhanced performance in handling domain shifts compared to baseline architectures. It emerges as an effective framework for leveraging unlabeled and unsupervised visual information in satellite imagery.

The segmentation of multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions in MRI is complicated by the high variability in lesion shapes and sizes, necessitating deep learning models that are resilient to variations in data distribution. While experience replay originally served as an agent-friendly strategy to enhance stability during reinforcement learning, the principles upon which it operates hold significant relevance for the supervised training of convolutional neural networks. This study introduces a novel adaptation of experience replay tailored specifically for MS lesion segmentation across datasets drawn from multiple hospitals to mitigate domain shifts. The proposed framework relies on two primary components: first, the storage of all intermediate model states from previous training iterations to ensure access to agent experience from prior domains; second, the utilization of ensemble predictions derived from these historical models to augment training samples. The effectiveness of this approach was validated through segmentation tasks on a challenging, public MRI dataset from the Multiple Sclerosis Image Analysis for Transfer Learning (MS-UL) initiative. The model's performance was evaluated using both the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity as well as Dice Similarity Coefficient. The results demonstrate that the experience replay framework significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods designed for cross-domain segmentation of MS lesions.

We introduce a method to fit a statistical model's parameters such that a specified theoretical distribution aligns closely with observed data. The paper applies this framework to two scenarios: approximating income data and call volume data. While the model consists of two components tailored to fit a log-normal distribution for the call and income data, we also examine a model capable of detecting bimodality.

We propose a novel learning algorithm for a full quantum state representation, which operates through the sequential and adaptive measurement of qubits. In this framework, every measurement step depends on the current qubit's index, the round number, and previously chosen measurement bases. While arbitrary quantum state learning is inherently impossible to achieve exactly, this algorithm successfully computes exact expectation values for a broad class of observables—those expressible using single-qubit Pauli operators, multi-qubit Pauli Z operators, or Clifford circuit-conjugated variants of these. Furthermore, these iterative steps yield strictly approximate results for other observables. Functioning as a maximum likelihood procedure that incorporates prior experimental data, these underlying invariants emerge as constraints on the likelihood function that drastically narrow the search space for initial angles, thereby enabling the efficient computation of maximum likelihood estimates.

We establish new asymptotic connections between the potentials with compact support arising in the monochromatic and causal Radon transforms employed in contemporary computerized tomography and geometrical optics. These relations represent an enhancement of earlier formulas found in literature, notably those by Kirsch and Neitzel (Inverse Problems 15 (1999), 1403-1415). Furthermore, we examine a scenario where the underlying potential possesses a compact support with a fractal boundary.

Imbalanced learning is a critical issue in machine learning that has spurred diverse research into generating synthetic minority samples. Among these approaches, Transmutation and Mixture techniques represent two distinct strategies. Transmutation assigns original class labels of neighboring majority samples to generated minority instances, whereas the Mixture technique combines feature vectors from both majority and existing minority samples to create new synthetic samples. This paper presents an extensive empirical evaluation of these methods across four public datasets and five specific metrics. The results indicate that Mixture outperforms Transmutation in overall metrics, although Transmutation yields superior performance under a balanced metric. Furthermore, Mixture's performance improvement diminishes with increasing dataset size, while its performance under the balanced metric correlates positively with the original dataset's class imbalance ratio. To address this limitation, we propose a new method called Mixture Transmutation, which integrates Mixture synthesis with Transmutation labeling. Our experiments demonstrate that Mixture Transmutation surpasses both traditional Transmutation and Mixture techniques in balance-sensitive metrics.

Multi-task learning is designed to address issues like sample inefficiency—a critical challenge when gathering data is costly—and prior statistical methodologies have primarily focused on discovering a shared latent structure to enhance learning outcomes. In contrast, this study examines models that utilize pre-discovered structures, such as those enabled by prior knowledge of graph connections, to estimate parameters across multiple potentially heterogeneous tasks. We present new sample-efficient rigorous guarantees for these affine combinations models and extend these results to solve a more complex, realistic objective: multi-task regression. Our approach and theoretical analysis are applicable to a broader spectrum of modern machine learning models. Notably this result represents the pioneering exact sample-efficiency proof for multi-task regression in any study to our knowledge. We substantiate our theoretical findings with extensive numerical experiments, specifically analyzing off-policy reinforcement learning—a demanding scenario where samples lack independence. Our success in this non-iid context relies on graph information combined with a specific weighting strategy that counteracts the detrimental effects of off-policy data sampling to ensure sample efficiency.

Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as a promising technique for accelerating large language models (LLMs) by minimizing the performance degradation caused by reducing precision levels. However, when applied to LLMs handling low-resource languages (LRMs), PTQ often yields less reliable results compared to Knowledge Distillation (KD). To address this inconsistency, we identify the distribution disparity between PTQ training data and real-world low-resource language data as a primary factor. Based on this insight, we introduce a proposed method designed to align low-resource language data distributions within the PTQ context, resulting in a new framework we call "Matched PTQ" (MPtQ). Our approach is straightforward, requiring no additional data during the process, and is effective for all types of data. Experiments on a highly complex PTB dataset demonstrate that our new method outperforms both standard PTQ and KD, achieving a 9.3% improvement in perplexity. Furthermore, evaluations on low-resource languages, including Chinese and Korean, result in PTQ matching the performance of KD, and in some cases, even surpassing it.

Baber and Talbot established that the Turán density for r-uniform graphs is exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ for odd values of $r$ by building on a lower bound previously derived by the second author regarding a no-threepath problem in $r$-uniform hypergraphs. Subsequently, in a separate paper, we demonstrated that this no-threepath problem is asymptotically bounded by a binomial coefficient. This result further clarifies the connection between these two theorems. The argument relies on a new approach utilizing generalized Turán numbers concerning uniform complete $k$-partite $k$-graphs. The bound result is achieved by integrating Gerbner's double counting technique with novel uniformity stability properties specific to $H$-free $H$-graphs. Furthermore, these generalized $H$-graph uniformity stability theorems are of independent interest.

This approach eliminates the need for manual labeling for the paired images, as it only requires labels for one image in each pair. Consequently, this method can reduce labeled data requirements up to 99% for one-class augmentation and up to 89% for two-one augmentation. Recent advancements demonstrate that integrating prompt learning into image captioning enhances performance by offering flexible near-human linguistic phrasing while preserving or improving existing models. Despite these benefits, naive application often results in suboptimal outcomes. Consequently, we present Prompt Captioning (PC), an innovative framework designed to deliver superior and diverse linguistic diversity alongside various cloze-based and benchmark captioning performance, even in suboptimal performance scenarios. The proposed approach delivers linguistic diversity comparable to human generation while achieving superior performance in various cloze-based and standard metrics for captioning, despite the absence of specific adjustments for each metric. Additionally, we provide an extensive empirical study analyzing the contributions of prompt design, the integration of CLIP, and the implementation of CLIP-based fine-tuning on these models to offer valuable insights for prompt engineering in image captioning tasks.

Wildlife conservation represents a significant global challenge, necessitating innovative strategies for researchers. This paper introduces a deep learning architecture applied to wildlife monitoring, which involves identifying animal species within image datasets. The proposed method utilizes Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to classify cats, dogs, and foxes, employing a specific framework of four sequential networks: two dedicated to extracting features from input images and two focused on predicting those features accurately. Additionally, the study incorporates the adversarial element known as the Feature Vector Normalization (FVN) layer, designed to regulate the distribution of activated features toward a uniform structure. Experimental outcomes indicate that this approach surpasses other leading methods on major benchmark repositories like ImageNet and CIFAR-10 while offering superior performance on Caltech Bird datasets specifically tailored for fox classification.

We introduce an unsupervised, two-stage approach to generate translations for speech in both zero- and few-shot scenarios. Initially, a neural speech translation model is trained using a large dataset of isolated utterance-pairs, which are automatically aligned using our specific method; these aligned data points serve as the zero-shot output. During the second stage, the model is fine-tuned on short, in-distribution utterances to achieve zero- and few-shot tasks. Results from automatic and manual human evaluations demonstrate that this method significantly enhances performance in few-shot settings compared to existing baselines and performs competitively in few-shot scenarios compared to methods relying on data from the same in-distribution.

Accurate energy load forecasting is vital for energy service companies to efficiently schedule generation, balance the grid, and minimize costs while energy pricing shifts to a time-of-use model based on demand prediction precision. Current industry standards typically employ regression analyses of historical consumption data, though these models often struggle to capture demand fluctuations during peak hours due to outliers. To address this, this study introduces a novel strategy that merges traditional forecasts with peak-optimized ones to enhance forecasting performance. By utilizing a linear combination architecture for the integration process, the research demonstrates using both models to boost overall accuracy. To implement this, the team developed a multi-objective optimization framework capable of generating this blending architecture automatically. The corresponding genetic algorithm is configured with multiple objectives to deliver a diverse portfolio of blending configurations, each designed to maximize performance during peak periods. To validate the approach, the team tested the generated blends on two distinct energy time-series datasets and contrasted their results against baseline individual models.

Recent advancements have integrated domain knowledge into machine learning to enhance algorithmic performance. However, prior approaches typically rely on data-driven, heuristic formulations of the prior distributions used for embedding this knowledge. Consequently, these methods struggle when specific data instances are absent, leading to priors that fail to accurately model missing contexts and degrade the effectiveness of resulting algorithms. To address these limitations, we present a novel technique for embedding general fact collections into priors for Bayesian Machine Learning via the systematic construction of logical rules and their corresponding priors. These intermediate priors, informed directly by the content of the fact base, replace traditional defaults. Our approach is implemented within the probabilistic programming language Stan, enabling precise, closed-form computations via Stan's algebra of priries. To demonstrate its utility, we applied this method to two practical scenarios—optimizing a logistic regression in computer vision tasks and enhancing Support Vector Machines for natural language processing—both yielding performance improvements that outperformed baseline models.

Accurately locating and characterizing anatomic abnormalities is a critical yet difficult challenge in medical imaging. This study introduces a data-driven framework that utilizes image-only labels to train a loss localization encoder. This encoders output serves as soft labels, which are then employed by standard localization losses, such as those based on object detection or image segmentation. To our best knowledge, this represents the first workflow demonstrating that a complex localization task—specifically identifying brain lesions from MRI scans—can be achieved by pre-training either a detection model or a segmentation network that predicts lesion masks using inputs derived solely from classification data. Consequently, this efficient pipeline significantly cuts down the effort required to curate dense labels for extensive training. Furthermore, this classification-dependent localization strategy is broadly adaptable, as it can be customized using various loss functions, detection models, or segmentation architectures.

This study examines how the coherence length of an incident electromagnetic (EM) wave affects the stability and lifetime of the resulting dark state within an absorption-free one-way waveguide. We demonstrate that the emergent dark state is not inherently immune to fluctuations; specifically, we show that the lifetime of both its constituent components— the zeroth-order transmitted state localized in the core and the first state that is primarily scattered—depends on the coherence properties of the incoming radiation. While incoherent noise tends to shorten lifetimes, in-phase coherent excitation significantly stabilizes both for long in-phase and first states associated with the core guidance and scattered modes, respectively.

Spring-actuated robots, which mimic spring-loaded biological organisms like insects and mammals, have recently seen significant development due to their energy-efficient and robust dynamic locomotion. This efficiency stems from the alignment of springs and compliant terrain springs during interaction; however, in legged systems, direct spring-to-spring engagement is less frequent than spring-to-force actuators because direct sensing requires precise knowledge of terrain compliance. This study introduces a practical method for robustly estimating ground conditions using existing force/torque sensors mounted on legs, which then guides the intelligent placement of leg spring couplings to optimize performance. Experimental tests across various scenarios confirm that this approach reliably infers soil properties and enhances the efficiency of locomotion on such varying terrains.

Although full state separability for arbitrary N-qubit systems is generally considered an NP-hard computational challenge, quantum-assisted approaches offer a potential pathway to resolution. This study introduces a hybrid-classic/quantum algorithm designed to determine if the hybrid-state classification for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware can operate on existing noisy equipment with $N$ qubits ($N \leq 19$). The design relies on an entanglement witness (EW) that serves as a sufficient condition for separability; this specific formulation maps directly onto a circuit compatible with near-term architectures. We further demonstrate that the hybrid-state classification may be refined by applying projected Hilbert space optimization (PHS-OPT) to the Lagrangian function. This approach allows researchers to employ entangimentary resources smaller than total qubits ($N-Q$) while simultaneously enhancing the witness's sensitivity and speed. Validation studies were performed using pure states, full separable states, various bipartite separable states, and nonfully separable states generated stochastically. Results indicate that applying PHS-OPT to the Lagrangian function enhances the witness's performance, enabling the detection of non-separability in states that remain undetected by the baseline PHS-OPT method. Finally, simulations confirm that this optimized PHS-OPT-based entangimentary witness functions effectively on a $5$-qubit IBMQ quantum processor, marking the first implementation of entangimentary detection using noisy hardware.

The effects of electron finite Larmor radius (FLR) dynamics on tearing parity instabilities driven by fine-scale magnetic structures have been investigated. This study examines a specific magnetic equilibrium defined by the profile $|\nabla B_0| \propto |x|^n$, where $n \in [0.5, 1.5]$. The analysis reveals that electron FLR contributions can either suppress or reverse the characteristics of the fine-scale tearing parity instabilities.

The challenge of fashion instance-level image retrieval (FIR) is gaining traction within the research community owing to its significant real-world potential. Existing methods typically rely on employing domain-specific datasets, which are often laborious to create. To address this labor-intensive issue, we propose a general framework that leverages data from non-fashion domains. In our approach, an off-the-shelf model is utilized to generate pseudo-queries from non-fashion images. These pseudo-queries are then refined using a multi-task learning system that fine-tuning a model on a modestly-sized FIR dataset. We validate the efficacy of this proposed method by applying it to create a high-quality FIR dataset of non-physical objects.

This study investigates an approximation strategy for infinite-dimensional ill-posed problems utilizing gradient flow methods. Since such ill-posed characteristics prevent the attainment of exact numerical solutions, particularly within finite computational times, an appropriate truncation or stopping time must be selected. As established by Eckart argumentation, however, no general convergence guarantee holds for all such problems in finite times. Consequently, selecting a suitable stopping time becomes critical for ensuring optimal outcomes. In this context, we demonstrate that specific regularity conditions for the initial data enable an optimal-rate adaptive choice of the stopping time. Furthermore, we establish that this adaptive selection achieves the best attainable convergence rates, which are dictated by the available prior information.

In this study, we introduce a deep learning-based cost constructor designed for monocular depth estimation. By utilizing the input RGB image, the network generates a cost volume tailored to a specific 3D slice of volume within a 3D space. This tailored volume can be further utilized in a 3D-slicing loop to reconstruct the entire volume within the estimated 3D space. In our network architecture, the depth map is generated from the best pixel-wise 3D-slicing plane that best fits the estimated volume, which helps resolve challenging issues such as occlusion. In addition to improving the quality of the depth estimation, the network can recover the prior knowledge of 3D object shapes to help resolve the occlusion. Extensive experimental results show that the network performs well in terms of quality of the predicted results and helps reduce depth estimation errors. The two-dimensional massive Thirring model, along with the Fokas-Lenells equation—a second two-dimensional integrable system that has been shown through transformation to be equivalent to each other—has been analyzed using the Fuchsian approach. This study introduces and utilizes a singular spectrum equation tailored for the two-dimensional massive Thrilling model to generate its solutions. By sifting out the solution's specific behavior at spatial infinity and assigning distinct spectral values based on mass, a novel framework emerges. This framework assigns a specific spectrum value to each of these values and subsequently employs a technique to determine a corresponding solution. This process effectively produces solutions that align with the results previously established by Daughton and others.

We investigate how to embed general relativity, $p$-form gauge theories, and Scherk-Schwarz twisted gauge theories into double field theory (DFT). For the former $p$-form case, this involves defining $p$-form gauge transformations within the DFT framework using coordinate systems where worldvolume coordinates adhere to specific relations outside the generic null-foliage manifold; in this regard, we offer illustrative examples on double null-foliage manifolds. Regarding Scherk-Schwarz gauge theories, we demonstrate that their gauge transformations can be encapsulated as DFT gauge transformations by adopting a specific local generalized Lie derivative derived from appropriate Lie derivatives of DFT, utilizing appropriate Killing vectors of the generalized metric linked to global or local isometries of that metric, or more generally from projections of such vectors onto $is$ of the double nonlinear ones.

This paper presents a channel load-aware user access selection method to enhance the performance of small-scale home networks by mitigating excessive channel switching and optimizing user channel assignment. The proposed mechanism selects the Access Point (AP) that offers the lowest channel load relative to RSSI and determines the optimal channel based on load-aware data rate predictions. Furthermore, we have developed channel switching optimization strategies to reduce inter-symbol interference and handover delays. Through extensive experimentation using a widely adopted Overture home network dataset, this work confirms that our channel selection method boosts user throughput by approximately 10% and reduces delay by 15% compared to traditional RSSI-driven associations. Additionally, channel switching refinements lead to a 17% decrease in delay and, when combined with load-aware rate selection, achieve throughput improvements up to 22%.
